15618.title: Control Remapping
15618.heading: Control Remapping
15618.content:
Control remapping lets players assign game actions and menu operations to preferred keys, buttons, or devices. It accommodates physical needs, learned habits, device differences, and conflicts among default assignments.

A remapping screen should show current assignments, unassigned actions, and available controls together. It should warn when required actions are missing, save profiles, and offer a way to restore defaults.

15621.title: Control Condition for Moral Responsibility
15621.heading: Control Condition for Moral Responsibility
15621.content:
The control condition for moral responsibility holds that a person can be responsible only when the relevant action or outcome was sufficiently under that person's control. AI complicates this condition because models adapt, systems interact, and automated decisions may occur faster than a human can intervene.

Control need not mean selecting every output personally. Organizations can exercise control through design choices, testing, access limits, monitoring, override procedures, and decisions about whether a system should be deployed. Designing these mechanisms is one way to prevent a [[Responsibility Gap]] rather than using autonomy as an excuse after harm occurs.

Contractual data control uses agreements to define who may access, copy, process, disclose, or transfer data. It can allocate responsibilities without creating a property right enforceable against everyone.

Contracts are flexible but normally bind only their parties, and bargaining power may determine their terms. They can therefore support data exchange while leaving collective interests or third-party effects unresolved.

15630.content:
A continuous variable transformation applies a mathematical function, such as a logarithm or square root, to every valid value. Analysts may use transformations to reduce skew, stabilize variance, or make a modeled relationship closer to linear.

The transformed distribution must be rechecked rather than assumed to improve. A log or square-root transformation can leave strong skewness intact, and its new scale may complicate interpretation even when it improves a diagnostic plot.

15633.title: Contracted Ideal
15633.heading: Contracted Ideal
15633.content:
Given a [[Ring Homomorphism]] f: R → T and an ideal J of T, the contracted ideal Jᶜ is the inverse image f⁻¹(J) in R. It contains exactly the source elements whose images lie in J.

For [[Ring Localization]], every ideal of the localized ring is the extension of its contraction. Prime ideals of the localization correspond to source primes disjoint from the denominator set.

The continuum assumption underlies ordinary aircraft analyses of [[Boundary Layers and Flow Separation]], pressure, lift, and drag.

15642.content:
Continuous speech recognition transcribes naturally connected speech without requiring pauses between words. The recognizer must infer boundaries while accounting for pronunciation changes caused by neighboring sounds.

The task requires sequence-aware [[Acoustic Model|acoustic models]], a [[Pronunciation Model]], and linguistic constraints from a [[Statistical Language Model]] to select among competing word sequences.

15645.title: Continuous Integration
15645.heading: Continuous Integration
15645.content:
Continuous integration merges small changes into the shared codebase frequently and verifies them with automated builds and tests. Failures are reported quickly and repaired before more work accumulates on an unstable base.

Its value is short integration feedback, not merely operating a build server. Small commits, dependable tests, and collective attention to broken builds keep the shared game usable.

For a React and ASP.NET Core application, an Azure DevOps build pipeline can trigger from the source repository, compile both applications, run automated tests, and publish versioned artifacts. This turns each accepted revision into rapid, repeatable evidence about whether it is ready to enter the release flow.

The design-patterns source applies the same cycle to several developers and branches: a code change triggers a new build, automated unit tests check it, and a failed build receives immediate attention before more changes accumulate. This is the integration gate before any environment-specific release decision.

15648.title: Continuous Improvement
15648.heading: Continuous Improvement
15648.content:
Continuous improvement repeatedly inspects how value is created, chooses a small change, and measures whether the system improves. Problems exposed by transparency become inputs to learning instead of reasons to conceal the real process.

A [[Sprint Retrospective]] creates a recurring cadence for this work, while Lean methods extend attention to the whole value stream. Improvement is part of delivery, not a separate initiative postponed until work is quiet.

15651.title: Continuous Deployment
15651.heading: Continuous Deployment
15651.content:
Continuous deployment automatically releases every change that passes the delivery pipeline to the live environment. It extends [[Continuous Delivery]] by removing the manual release decision from the normal flow.

Because games can have platform, player, and experiential constraints, teams may use staged exposure or feature toggles instead. The principle is to make deployment small, repeatable, observable, and reversible.

An Azure DevOps pipeline can remove routine manual execution by triggering a build, publishing an artifact, and advancing automated deployment stages when their checks pass. Whether production promotion is automatic determines whether this is continuous deployment rather than continuous delivery.

The design-patterns source describes different promotion triggers for development, user-acceptance testing, and production. Automated build and test gates can move a change toward release, but an explicit human sign-off before production makes that final stage continuous delivery rather than automatic deployment.

15654.title: Continuous Delivery
15654.heading: Continuous Delivery
15654.content:
Continuous delivery keeps the game in a deployable state and makes releases frequent, routine decisions. Automated building, testing, configuration, and deployment preparation reduce the risk and transaction cost of each release.

Delivery does not mean every verified change is automatically exposed to players. It ensures that the team can choose to deploy without a separate destabilizing integration phase.

In the book's Azure flow, versioned build artifacts enter a release pipeline and are deployed to a staging environment before production promotion. Environment configuration stays outside the artifact, allowing the same tested package to remain ready for a deliberate release decision.

The design-patterns source describes development, user-acceptance testing, and production as distinct promotion boundaries. Builds and checks can be automated while production still requires a scheduled or approved release, preserving a deployable artifact without claiming every passing change is live.

15657.heading: Continuous Collision Detection
15657.content:
Continuous collision detection determines whether moving shapes intersect at any time during an update interval rather than only at its endpoints. It can report a time of impact before objects penetrate or tunnel through each other.

The additional computation is valuable for fast objects and thin geometry. [[Swept Sphere Collision]] is one continuous method that treats motion as a volume traced across time.

15663.heading: Continuity Equation for Fluid Flow
15663.content: The continuity equation expresses conservation of mass in a flowing fluid: $\rho Av$ has the same value through every cross-section of a steady flow tube. For an incompressible fluid, density is constant and the relation becomes $A_1v_1=A_2v_2$. Fluid therefore moves faster through a narrower section.

15669.title: Contingency Table
15669.heading: Contingency Table
15669.content:
A contingency table cross-classifies observations by the levels of two categorical variables. Its cells contain joint frequencies, while margins summarize the totals for each row and column.

The table supports inspection of sparse cells and calculation of [[Row Proportion|row]], [[Column Proportion|column]], and total proportions. It is also the data object on which tests such as the [[Pearson Chi-Squared Test]] and [[Fisher Exact Test]] operate.

15672.content:
Contextual fit means software aligns with the existing practices, norms, and environment of its users rather than merely checking off formal requirements. The system feels like a coherent extension of work people already know how to do.

Achieving fit requires immersion and feedback. Designers must understand the relationships and constraints that users may find too obvious to mention in a requirements interview.

15675.title: Context-Specific Language
15675.heading: Context-Specific Language
15675.content: Context-specific language gives a term one unambiguous meaning within a defined setting. A product can mean sales price and margin in sales, stock and availability in inventory, or storage size and location in a warehouse. Forcing all meanings into one universal object creates optional fields, tangled dependencies, and constant mental switching. A [[Ubiquitous Language]] should therefore remain consistent inside a context while allowing another context to use the same word differently.

15678.heading: Context-Rule Cohesion
15678.content:
Context-rule cohesion is the degree to which a game's presentation supports the behavior of its rules. When objects act according to the metaphors assigned to them, players can transfer prior expectations and predict new interactions.

When presentation suggests one behavior but the system produces another, the player may doubt the entire [[Player Mental Model]]. Cohesion can be strengthened through consistent imagery, motion, sound, timing, and [[Feedback]].

15681.title: Context-Free Language
15681.heading: Context-Free Language
15681.content:
A context-free language is a [[Formal Language]] generated by some [[Context-Free Grammar]]. Different grammars may generate the same language, including grammars that differ in ambiguity or suitability for mechanical parsing.

Context-free languages strictly include the regular languages: for example, a grammar can generate matched counts such as aⁿbⁿ, which the [[Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages]] shows is not regular. [[Pushdown Automaton|Pushdown automata]] recognize exactly the context-free languages.

15684.sourceSearchName: context free grammar context free grammar
15684.title: Context-Free Grammar
15684.heading: Context-Free Grammar
15684.content:
A context-free grammar describes how symbols can be combined using production rules. Terminal symbols correspond to words or tokens, while nonterminal symbols represent categories such as phrases, slots, or requests.

For a narrow assistant domain, a grammar can both recognize valid utterances and construct a [[Meaning Representation]]. Coverage and maintenance become difficult as users introduce unanticipated wording.

Formally, a context-free grammar is a four-tuple containing nonterminal symbols, terminal symbols, [[Production Rule|production rules]], and a start symbol. Starting from that symbol, a [[Derivation]] generates a language by repeatedly replacing a nonterminal without regard to its surrounding context.

15687.title: Context Map
15687.heading: Context Map
15687.content: A context map describes the landscape of [[Bounded Context]]s and the relationships through which they exchange information. Early evidence can appear in [[EventStorming]] when groups form separate event clusters joined by only a few cross-boundary events. The map makes dependencies visible without merging the internal models. It supports decisions about ownership, translation, integration, and the direction in which one context depends on another.

15690.heading: Context-Content Coupling

Preserving the coupling can reveal semantic and pragmatic functions that frequency alone misses. It also makes analysis more demanding because variation must be investigated rather than removed as noise.

15693.content:
A context design value identifies who will play, where and when play will occur, how people will encounter the game, and why they may choose to participate. These conditions affect session length, explanation, controls, privacy, social behavior, and expectations.

Treating context as a value keeps the imagined use situation visible during iteration. A game designed for a noisy public event requires different signals and commitments from one intended for solitary, repeated play.

15696.heading: Content-Driven Game
15696.content:
A content-driven game relies primarily on authored sequences of levels, events, dialogue, or other material to carry the player forward. Its experience tends to follow a limited set of intended paths.

Because each additional experience requires more authored content, the approach can create a content treadmill and limited replayability. It contrasts with a [[Systemic Game]], though most games combine authored content with systemic structure.

15699.heading: Content-Based Recommendation
15699.content:
Content-based recommendation suggests items whose features resemble items a user liked in the past. Similarity is calculated from item attributes, such as terms in a document or other descriptive properties.

The method can operate without preferences from other users, but it is limited by the quality of the item representation and may repeatedly recommend things too similar to what is already known.

15702.title: Content-Based Misinformation Detection
15702.heading: Content-Based Misinformation Detection
15702.content:
Content-based misinformation detection uses properties of the message itself, such as words, topics, sentiment, style, or repeated URLs. These features are transformed into a representation from which a classifier estimates a label.

Content can expose recurring deceptive patterns but may be imitated or change rapidly. Combining it with network and account evidence can reduce dependence on any single clue.

15705.title: Content Popularity
15705.heading: Content Popularity
15705.content:
Content popularity is the amount of attention or interaction a social item receives. It may be operationalized through views, visits, votes, comments, shares, retweets, or another behavior appropriate to the platform.

The measure is time-dependent: a high final count, a rapid early burst, and sustained attention describe different outcomes. A prediction must therefore state both its popularity measure and its forecast horizon.

15707.sourceSearchName: consumption based pricing consumption based pricing
15707.title: Consumption-Based Pricing
15707.heading: Document

15708.sourceSearchName: consumption based pricing consumption based pricing
15708.title: Consumption-Based Pricing
15708.heading: Consumption-Based Pricing
15708.content:
Consumption-based pricing charges for the computing resources actually used over a period. Common measures include storage capacity, processing power, memory, and network bandwidth.

The model aligns naturally with infrastructure and platform services because their resource consumption is visible. It is less meaningful for a consumer of information or a business process, who normally cares about the delivered information or transaction rather than the processors used behind it.

15709.sourceSearchName: consumption based pricing consumption based pricing
15709.title: Consumption-Based Pricing
15709.heading: References

15711.title: Content Lifecycle
15711.heading: Content Lifecycle
15711.content:
A content lifecycle is the time pattern through which an item gains, sustains, and loses attention. Different kinds of social content can decline immediately, remain steady, rebound after an initial drop, or burst and disappear quickly.

Lifecycle features allow a model to distinguish transient trends from durable interest. Early observations become more informative when interpreted against the characteristic shape of the content type.

15714.title: Container Orchestration
15714.heading: Container Orchestration
15714.content:
Container orchestration coordinates deployment, placement, scaling, networking, and recovery for groups of containers. Instead of starting every process manually, an operator declares the desired workload and the orchestrator continuously reconciles actual state with it.

In the AKS example, changing a replica count causes more worker pods to appear, and deleting a pod causes a replacement to be created. Automation turns failure recovery and scale-out into controlled platform behavior.

15716.sourceSearchName: container dependency isolation container dependency isolation
15716.title: Container Dependency Isolation

15717.sourceSearchName: container dependency isolation container dependency isolation
15717.title: Container Dependency Isolation
15717.heading: Container Dependency Isolation
15717.content:
Container dependency isolation packages the versions required by an application so they do not depend on shared global installation state on the destination machine. This reduces conflicts in which two programs require incompatible versions of the same library or system component.

The book traces this motivation from registered DLLs and the global assembly cache through virtual machines to containers. An image captures the tested application environment without carrying a complete independently maintained guest operating system.

15720.title: Consumer Privacy Paradox
15720.heading: Consumer Privacy Paradox
15720.content:
The consumer privacy paradox is the gap between expressed concern about privacy and behavior that still discloses personal information. Mobile users may accept tracking because a service offers convenience, access, social value, status, or a monetary benefit.

The gap does not necessarily prove that privacy is unimportant. Choices can be constrained by unclear notices, limited alternatives, trust, habits, or difficulty evaluating future uses of data.

15721.title: Consumer Privacy Paradox

15723.title: Consumer Data Broker
15723.heading: Consumer Data Broker
15723.content:
A consumer data broker aggregates information from multiple sources and resells or applies the combined records. Mobile applications and websites can supply behavioral data that brokers connect with other databases.

The resulting profiles may be used for identity verification, marketing, or fraud detection. Aggregation increases usefulness while making it harder for a person to know which data exist, how they were interpreted, and who can act on them.

15729.title: Constructible Number
15729.heading: Constructible Number
15729.content:
A constructible number is a coordinate obtainable from the rational starting configuration by straightedge-and-compass steps. Intersections of lines and circles create a tower of field extensions of degree one or two.

Consequently, its degree over the rationals must be a power of two.

Constant time complexity, written $O(1)$, means that an operation needs no more than a fixed amount of work regardless of [[Input Size]]. Checking whether the last digit of an integer is odd or even is constant time because the rest of the digits need not be examined.

Constant time is the fastest complexity family discussed in the source. The notation does not require one literal step; it permits any fixed number of steps that does not grow with $n$.

15762.title: Constant Term
15762.heading: Constant Term
15762.content:
A constant term is an [[Algebraic Term]] whose value does not depend on a variable. In (3x^2-5x+7), the term (7) is constant.

Constants behave as like terms with other constants, so they can be combined during [[Algebraic Simplification]]. Their role depends on the surrounding form. In a linear expression (ax+b), (b) shifts the value independently of (x); in a polynomial, the constant is the term of degree zero. Writing it explicitly can also preserve place structure during [[Polynomial Long Division]].

15819.title: Confusion Matrix
15819.heading: Confusion Matrix
15819.content:
A confusion matrix counts how often each actual class is assigned to each predicted class. For a chosen positive class, its cells yield true positives, false positives, false negatives, and true negatives.

Those counts support accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, and F-measure. Inspecting the matrix is especially important when one class is rare because a high overall accuracy can conceal failure to identify that class.

The book derives held-out counts from predicted and observed classes, then uses them to interpret precision, recall, and the F-measure. Keeping the chosen positive class explicit prevents the same table from being read in contradictory ways.

15831.title: Confounding Variable
15831.heading: Confounding Variable
15831.content:
A confounding variable is associated with both an exposure and an outcome without lying on the causal pathway between them. If it is not controlled, the observed exposure–outcome association may partly reflect the confounder's influence.

Candidate confounders should be selected from subject-matter knowledge and prior evidence before examining the target association. A variable is not established as a confounder merely because its own regression coefficient is statistically significant.

The source shows the corresponding design-matrix failure when treatment and sex are perfectly aligned. Balancing the factor combinations restores full rank, allowing the treatment and sex effects to be estimated separately rather than attributing their shared pattern arbitrarily.

The temperature gradient points toward the direction of greatest temperature increase, while conductive heat flux points oppositely. In three-dimensional Cartesian space, separate temperature derivatives in $x$, $y$, and $z$ define the components of this vector relationship.

Total conductive power through a surface uses the component normal to that surface. Thus an $x$-directed heat flux crosses a plane parallel to $y$ and $z$, a geometric relationship that must be preserved in boundary selections and [[COMSOL Point Line and Surface Evaluations|surface evaluations]].

15840.title: Conditioned Scatterplot
15840.heading: Conditioned Scatterplot
15840.content: A conditioned scatterplot divides observations into panels according to one or more conditioning variables and plots the same relationship within each subset. Time-derived factors such as month expose how an association changes seasonally. Additional panels may distinguish alternative statistics or transformations. Consistent scales support comparison, while transparency, rugs, and smoothers can reveal distribution and shape within each panel without collapsing the subsets into a single average relationship.

15843.title: Confidence Interval
15843.heading: Confidence Interval
15843.content:
A confidence interval combines a [[Point Estimate]] with a margin determined by its [[Standard Error]] and a reference distribution. It reports a range of parameter values compatible with the procedure's sampling uncertainty.

The confidence level is a long-run property: across repeated samples, the stated proportion of intervals will contain the fixed parameter. A particular interval does not assign that probability to the parameter after the data are observed.

15846.title: Conditional Sensor Dependence
15846.heading: Conditional Sensor Dependence
15846.content:
Conditional sensor dependence remains when two readings share influences even after the primary hidden state is known. Treating those readings as independent can count related evidence more than once and make the fused distribution too confident.

A model can retain a joint factor for a dependent sensor group or introduce another hidden variable explaining their correlation. The richer structure increases parameter and inference cost but better represents the information sources.

15849.title: Conditional Survival Table
15849.heading: Conditional Survival Table
15849.content:
A conditional survival table lists event times, the number at risk just before each time, the number of events, the estimated survival probability, and often its standard error. It is the numerical structure behind a Kaplan–Meier curve.

The table shows why survival probability is not a fixed-period prevalence. Participants can leave the risk set through events or censoring, causing the denominator for each conditional step to change.

15852.title: Conditional Proposition
15852.heading: Conditional Proposition
15852.content:
The conditional proposition p → q states that if p is true, then q is true. It is false only when its antecedent p is true and its consequent q is false, and it is [[Logically Equivalent]] to ¬p ∨ q.

Its converse q → p is generally different, while its contrapositive ¬q → ¬p is equivalent to the original conditional. This equivalence supports [[Proof by Contrapositive]].

15855.title: Conditional Information Bottleneck Clustering
15855.heading: Conditional Information Bottleneck Clustering
15855.content:
Conditional information bottleneck clustering compresses observations into cluster labels that preserve information about a target representation while conditioning out information already captured by a known clustering. The objective formalizes a distinct yet informative view.

Tradeoff parameters balance compression, relevance, and novelty. Estimating mutual information from limited or high-dimensional data can be difficult, and an information-theoretic difference still needs domain interpretation.

15858.title: Conditional Random Field Classification
15858.heading: Conditional Random Field Classification
15858.content:
Conditional random field classification models the conditional distribution of a connected label set given observed features. It avoids specifying a separate generative distribution for the observations.

Feature functions can depend on neighboring labels and the evidence, making the model well suited to structured predictions such as labeling every position in a sequence. Training and inference remain coupled to the graph structure and may require dynamic programming or approximation.

15861.title: Conditional Probability
15861.heading: Conditional Probability
15861.content:
Conditional probability describes the probability of one proposition or variable given that specified information is known. In $P(X \mid Y)$, $X$ is the queried event and $Y$ is the conditioning knowledge.

Conditioning changes the relevant distribution rather than merely selecting a label. It lets a probabilistic model express how evidence about one variable alters what can be inferred about another.

15864.title: Conditional Independence
15864.heading: Conditional Independence
15864.content:
Variables $X$ and $Y$ are conditionally independent given $Z$ when knowing $Y$ adds no information about $X$ once $Z$ is known: $P(X \mid Y,Z)=P(X \mid Z)$.

This is weaker and more useful than unconditional independence. Bayesian decomposition uses conditional independence to replace a large joint distribution with smaller factors, reducing inference and learning cost while retaining dependencies explained through the conditioning variables.

15867.title: Conditional Equation
15867.heading: Conditional Equation
15867.content:
A conditional equation is an equality that is true only for particular values of its variables. The equation (4+x=6-x) is true when (x=1) but false for most real values.

Those particular values form the [[Solution of an Equation]]. A conditional equation contrasts with an [[Algebraic Identity]], which remains true for every allowed assignment, and with an inconsistent assertion that has no solution. Solving uses equality-preserving transformations to isolate the unknown and then checks the result in the original condition.

15870.title: Conditional Expectation
15870.heading: Conditional Expectation
15870.content:
A conditional expectation is the mean of an outcome among cases with specified predictor values, written as $E(Y\mid X=x)$. Under squared-error loss, it is the prediction that minimizes expected error for those predictor values.

For a binary outcome coded zero and one, the conditional expectation equals the conditional probability of class one. This connects regression-style estimation to [[Bayesian Classification]] and other class-prediction methods.
